title: Design HashSet
description: Brute force to optimized: a single flat list scanned linearly versus hashing with chaining across an array of small buckets.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a HashSet without using any built-in hash table libraries. Support add(key) (insert if not present), remove(key) (remove if present), and contains(key) (return whether the key exists).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Implement a hash set without built-in hash structures\"","Build hashing with chaining manually: an array of buckets, each a small list"],["Keys bounded in a known range","A simple modulo-based hash function distributes keys evenly across buckets"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A hash set needs to support fast insertion, deletion, and membership testing. Without a built-in hash table, this needs to be built manually: a hash function maps each key to a "bucket," and each bucket holds a small list of the keys that landed there, keeping each operation's cost proportional to a bucket's size rather than the whole set's size.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting Mail into Numbered Cubbyholes
blocks.text: Picture sorting mail into a wall of numbered cubbyholes, where each piece of mail's destination cubbyhole is determined by a simple rule (like the last few digits of an ID). Finding, adding, or removing a piece of mail only requires checking the ONE cubbyhole it would be in, not the entire wall.

blocks.caption: A hash function maps each key to one bucket; only that bucket needs to be searched

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: add(1), add(2), contains(1), contains(3), add(2), contains(2), remove(2), contains(2)
Results: null, null, true, false, null, true, null, false. Adding 2 twice has no extra effect (it was already present); after removing 2, contains(2) correctly returns false.
5. How Should We Think?

Before using one giant list scanned linearly for every operation, notice that distributing keys across many smaller "buckets" using a simple hash function (like key modulo bucket count) means each operation only needs to search within one small bucket, not the entire set.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A single flat list requires scanning up to the ENTIRE set for add (checking for duplicates), remove, and contains, an O(n) cost per operation in the worst case.

Observation 2: If keys are distributed across many buckets using a hash function, and keys distribute roughly evenly, each bucket holds only a small fraction of the total keys.

Observation 3: A simple and effective hash function here is key modulo (a fixed, reasonably large prime-ish bucket count), which spreads keys out reasonably evenly across buckets.

Observation 4: Within a bucket (a small list), add checks for duplicates before inserting, remove finds and deletes the matching entry, and contains just checks for the key's presence, all only within that one bucket.

This leads to an array of buckets (each a small list), with a modulo-based hash function to determine which bucket a key belongs to, keeping each operation's cost proportional to a single bucket's size rather than the whole set.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain a single flat list of all keys currently in the set, scanning it linearly for every operation.
Step by step algorithm

items: add(key): scan the list; if key is not already present, append it.
remove(key): scan the list for key; if found, remove it.
contains(key): scan the list for key, returning whether it was found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A single flat list directly implements set semantics, easy to reason about.
Every operation costs O(n) in the worst case, scanning the whole list, too slow for 10^4 calls on a large set.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per operation, n being the current set size.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: distributing keys across many buckets via hashing reduces each operation's cost to roughly O(n / bucket count) on average, approximating O(1) with a well-chosen bucket count.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning the entire set is wasteful: only keys that HASH to the same bucket as the target key could possibly match it, so scanning the other buckets is unnecessary.

Choosing the hash function: key modulo a fixed bucket count (a moderately large number, larger than the expected number of distinct keys, to keep buckets small on average) is simple and effective for this problem's bounded key range.

Handling collisions: multiple keys can hash to the SAME bucket (a "collision"), so each bucket is itself a small list ("chaining"), and add/remove/contains operate within that one list only.

The core idea: hashing with chaining, distributing keys across an array of buckets so each operation only needs to search a small fraction of the total keys.

Maintain an array of buckets, each a small list, sized generously beyond the expected key count. Hash a key via key modulo bucket count; add, remove, and contains operate only within that one bucket's list.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run with bucket count 1009

blocks.caption: Hashing with chaining: an array of buckets, each a small list, keeps operations fast

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since the hash function deterministically maps every key to exactly one bucket, a key can only ever be found in that ONE bucket, never any other. This means every operation only needs to examine that one (typically small) bucket rather than the entire set, and with a reasonably large, fixed bucket count relative to the expected number of distinct keys, each bucket stays small on average, keeping operations close to O(1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n / bucket count) average per operation, approximating O(1) for a well-chosen bucket count relative to n.
Space: O(bucket count + n) for the buckets and stored keys.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Design HashSet is the foundational exercise in implementing hashing with chaining manually: a hash function to pick a bucket, and small per-bucket lists to resolve collisions, approximating O(1) average operations.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing too small a bucket count, causing many keys to collide into the same bucket and degrading performance toward the flat-list approach.

Forgetting to check for existing membership before adding (which would allow duplicate entries in a bucket, though harmless for set semantics if contains and remove account for it, it is cleaner to prevent duplicates outright).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["remove() called on a key never added","No effect, since the key is not found in its bucket."],["add() called twice with the same key","The second call has no effect, since the key is already present."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly discussing the bucket-count-versus-collision trade-off, and mentioning that a real hash table would dynamically resize buckets as load increases, shows depth beyond just implementing the basic chaining mechanism.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "implement a hash table from scratch", think: an array of buckets (chaining), each a small list, selected via a modulo-based hash function.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you dynamically resize the bucket array as the number of keys grows, to keep buckets small (like a real hash table)?
How would you design a HashMap (key-value pairs) using this same chaining technique?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Design HashMap, essentially identical but storing key-value pairs instead of just keys.
Any "implement a fundamental data structure from scratch" design problem, testing understanding of the structure's internal mechanics.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The flat-list approach runs in O(n) time per operation; the hashing-with-chaining approach runs in O(n / bucket count) average time per operation, approximating O(1) with a well-chosen bucket count.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: hashing with chaining, the fundamental technique behind hash table implementations.
Core Idea: a modulo-based hash function picks one of many buckets; each bucket is a small list resolving any collisions.
Time: O(n) per operation for the flat-list approach, O(n / bucket count) average for the chaining approach.
Most Important Observation: distributing keys across many buckets via hashing means each operation only ever needs to search one small bucket.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational exercise in understanding how hash tables work internally.
One line memory trick: hash to pick a bucket, then operate only within that small bucket.
